subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A teacher gives a short quiz every week purely to identify which concepts need re-teaching, without recording marks on the report card. This is an example of:
explanation: Formative assessment happens during learning to give feedback and guide instruction (assessment FOR learning). Summative assessment (e.g. a final exam) evaluates learning at the end of a unit for grading/certification (assessment OF learning).

section: Educational Psychology · Ch13 — Assessment, Evaluation & CCE
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A test that reports a student's score as 'mastered 8 out of 10 specified learning objectives', regardless of how other students performed, is:
explanation: Criterion-referenced tests measure performance against a fixed standard/objective (mastery of specific content), independent of peer performance. Norm-referenced tests compare a student's score to the performance of a reference group (e.g. percentile rank).

stem: Under Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation (CCE), a pupil's participation in sports, art and value-based activities is assessed under the:
explanation: CCE assesses two domains — scholastic (academic subjects) and co-scholastic (life skills, attitudes, values, sports, art, work education) — reflecting the 'comprehensive' aspect of the scheme.

stem: After noticing that several pupils consistently make the same subtraction error, a teacher designs a special test to pinpoint the exact misconception. This is:
explanation: Diagnostic evaluation identifies specific learning difficulties/misconceptions for remediation. Placement evaluation happens before instruction begins (e.g. to group students); summative evaluation is a terminal judgment of achievement.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch13 — Assessment, Evaluation & CCE
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A weighing scale that consistently shows 2 kg more than a person's actual weight, every single time, is:
explanation: Reliability means consistency of measurement (the same error every time = consistent = reliable); validity means measuring what it claims to measure accurately. A consistently wrong instrument is reliable but not valid — a key testing-theory distinction.
